Evidence for global warming
Describe the natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced greenhouse effect in terms of temperature and water vapour.









Research what albedo is and how it impacts global warming.







According to the map, China and the United States are among the highest contributors of carbon dioxide emissions. Australia, by contrast, has relatively low carbon dioxide emissions. Considering this information, suggest whether you think Australia needs to reduce its carbon emissions. Explain your answer.












Climate change is often debated in the media. Climate change sceptics deny it exists or that it is a problem, supporting the idea that changes are part of a natural cycle. Others believe that the world as we know it will end soon if we do not make hasty changes to our behaviour. Most citizens do not know enough about the evidence to judge one way or the other.Do you believe that climate change is an issue? Which sources of evidence and data do you trust the most and why? Do you believe your local, state and federal politicians? What agendas do the different groups within society have?Discuss these points with family and friends and share the key issues with your classmates.






Ice cores provide essential data, which has aided in the development of the graph.


Explain why ice cores are used to gather this data.






Explain what scientists look for in ice cores to collect data.

Uses of the electromagnetic spectrum
Key terms
critical angle
the angle of light that causes the reflected ray to move along the edge between two materials
optic fibre
a thin fibre of glass or plastic that carries information/data in the form of light
total internal reflection
the complete reflection of a light ray when it passes from a more dense to a less dense material at a large angle; the ray is reflected back into the dense medium 
Give an example of when total internal reflection is used.

Draw a diagram to illustrate how refraction and total internal reflection occur. You may wish to use Figure 1b from the lesson to help you.


Sequence the order of events below for when light passes through a prism.
Light travels from the light source through air (a less dense medium).
Light travels from the air into a prism (more dense medium).
Light can be refracted out of the prism into the air (less dense medium).
Light can be refracted within the prism at an angle greater than the critical angle where it is refracted back into the prism (dense medium) one or more times.
Light is then refracted back out of the prism into the air (less dense medium). 

What happens when light rays pass into a less dense medium at a very large angle?


What is this phenomenon called?

What is the angle of incidence at which total internal reflection occurs?

Extend your understanding
In 1919, Edwin Hubble was working on the Hooker telescope in Los Angeles. He used a spectrograph to look through the telescope at the galaxies and could relate what he found to the Doppler effect. The Doppler effect is the change in frequency of a wave for an observer moving relative to its source. What this means is that, if you are standing on a road and a car drives past you, the car will sound different when it approaches compared to when it is moving away.
When a car moves towards you, do you hear a high- or low-pitched sound?

Oxford Sciences 9 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet
Riderless bikes
In this module, you have been learning about how your body detects changes in its environment and uses a type of feedback signal to respond. Many engineering systems work in a similar way, detecting changes and responding to a feedback signal. 
Heater thermostats work on this principle. As they heat the air around them, they measure the air temperature, which becomes a feedback signal. When this signal indicates that the temperature is above or below a preset level, the heater responds by switching off or on. 
In this task, you will explore another common mechanical engineering system that you may be surprised to learn responds to its environment – a bicycle. 
When a human rides a bike, we use our biological control systems to help stay upright. When we sense we are falling to one side, our cerebellum is alerted, and we shift our body a little to the other side to rebalance. But how does a bike stay upright without a rider? 

Investigate centres of gravity
Aim
To investigate how changing the centre of gravity affects the stability of a riderless bicycle
Equipment:
An old bicycle (make sure the handlebar shaft slopes backwards  – most do)
A small hill with open space at the bottom
A 2–4 kg weight (e.g. a dumbbell)
Cloth bag
Duct tape
Measuring tape

Part A
Method
Setting the handlebars straight to begin with, push the bike down the hill as fast as you can. You may need to run with it for a short distance. The bike should stay upright for quite a while. Use a measuring tape to measure the distance the bike travels before it falls over. Repeat this “hill push” two more times. (Note: Try to ensure the bike is pushed with the same starting speed in each trial.)
Record your results in the table in the Data and results section. Calculate the average of your measurements. 
Lock the handlebars in place, so the wheel is in line with the bike frame but cannot turn. You can use duct tape or rope to do this. Push the bike down the hill with locked handlebars and measure the distance it travels. Repeat the “hill push” another two times. 
Record your results in the table in the Data and results section. Calculate the average of your measurements. 
Reflect
Did you notice the shorter distance before the bike fell over with the handlebars locked? Before reading on, discuss with a partner why you think this happens and write down your ideas.



Part B
The reason the bike stays upright for longer with free-moving handlebars is that handlebar movement is part of the feedback loop that controls this engineering system. When a moving bike starts to lean to one side, the handlebars flop to that side a little, which steers the front wheel towards the lean. When this happens, the direction of the bike changes and the front wheel comes back underneath the middle of the bike (in line with the centre of gravity) and it is balanced again. 
You may like to take a video from behind of your bike travelling down the hill and watch it in slow motion to help you understand this effect.
You are now going to explore how changing the centre of gravity of a bike affects this riderless bike control system.
Method
Examine your bike and identify three locations for your weight to be attached – one near the front, one near the middle and one near the rear of your bike. Make sure these locations are along the centreline of the bike (i.e. not at the ends of the handlebars or pedals). Adding weight towards the front of your bike will shift the centre of gravity forwards. Adding weight towards the rear will shift it backwards. 
Show the three locations you have chosen on the diagrams in the Data and results section.

Oxford Sciences 9 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet
Catching illegal wildlife traders
The short-beaked echidna (Tachyglossus aculeatus) is a well-known Australian monotreme. It is featured on the 5-cent coin. Found across almost all Australian habitats, from snowy mountains to deserts, it can be recognised by the quills on its back. These quills are modified hairs that can be up to 5 centimetres long.
The echidna uses smell to detect ants, termites, and other invertebrates. It has sharp claws that it uses to pull apart logs and dig into ant and termite nests. It uses its long, sticky tongue to catch insects and grind them against the roof of its mouth.
When threatened by cats, foxes, dogs, dingoes, or goannas, the echidna rolls into a ball or digs into the ground, exposing only its quills. 
Breeding occurs once a year (from June to September). The female lays a single soft-shelled egg (about the size of a grape) that hatches after 10 days in her pouch. The baby, called a puggle, is blind and hairless, and feeds off milk that is secreted onto the fur in the mother’s pouch. When the baby develops its quills, the mother leaves it in a burrow. She returns every few days to feed it until the baby is about seven months old.
Short-beaked echidnas are a protected species in Australia. This makes it illegal to capture or trade them. Unfortunately, they are highly prized in many zoos around the world. This means many illegal wildlife traders sell wild echidnas as “captive-bred”.
To combat this, scientists use a range of testing techniques, including high-resolution X-ray fluorescence and stable isotope analysis, to examine the keratin that makes up the echidna quills. This keratin is similar to the molecules found in human hair and nails. As the quills grow, they carry a record of the diet of the animal over time. 
Explain why some researchers describe an echidna’s quill as a time capsule.




Using the drawing of a quill below, describe where you might find information about:
The diet of the echidna in the previous few weeks 
The diet of the echidna several months ago  

High-resolution X-ray fluorescence shines high-energy X-rays at the echidna quill. The energy of the X-ray causes the atoms within the hair to become excited and emit their own forms of energy. The amounts and intensity of these secondary levels of energy can be measured and used to detect how much of a particular element is present in the hair.
Compare the radiation levels of alpha, beta, and gamma radiation.




Identify which type of radiation is most likely to be used for the high-resolution X-ray fluorescence process. Justify your answer.





The echidna’s quills were sampled at every 200 μm for 24 elements.
Explain why the quills had to be washed before they were tested.





The researchers found that there was a difference in the element levels between wild echidnas and captive echidnas. Captive echidnas had more variable element patterns than wild echidnas because the zoos provided many different types of foods that would not always be found in the wild. In contrast, wild echidnas were more likely to eat only the foods that were found in their local environment.

Oxford Sciences 9 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet
Spectrometer 
When the different wavelengths of light are separated out, we see the emission spectrum of the light. 
The instrument that is used to observe emission spectra is called a spectrometer. In its simplest form, a spectrometer consists of a box with two key elements: 
a slit to produce a thin parallel light beam
a diffraction grating that spreads out the different colours in the light beam by wavelength. 
Electrons move around the nucleus of an atom in spaces that are at set distances from the nucleus. These spaces are known as electron shells. Different elements absorb and emit different wavelengths of light depending on the number and location of electrons in their electron shells. Spectrometers can be used to identify elements based on their emission spectrum. 
Build a simple spectrometer
Aim
To build a simple spectrometer and use it to investigate the emission spectrum of sodium
Equipment
A thin box, such as a cereal box
A Stanley knife
A piece of diffraction grating
Sticky tape
Aluminium foil
Graph paper
Method
Use the Stanley knife to cut a small square hole in the top of the box. The square should be approximately 1 cm x 1 cm. This is the viewing hole.
Put the piece of diffraction grating inside the box so that it covers the viewing hole. Secure it with sticky tape.
On the bottom of the box, directly opposite the viewing hole, cut a vertical slit that is approximately 0.5 mm wide. This slit must have straight, sharp edges. If you are having trouble creating straight, sharp edges, take a piece of aluminium foil and fold it twice to create a sharp edge. Do this twice. Place the two pieces of folded foil at the location of the slit, making sure there is a 0.5 mm gap between them. Secure them with sticky tape.

Keep your graph paper handy. You will need it soon.
Pick up the box and point the slit at a light source (for example, a light globe). Look through the viewing hole, towards the slit. You should see an emission spectrum beside the slit. If you don’t, the diffraction grating may not be aligned correctly. Try rotating the diffraction grating by 90°.
Investigate how a spectrometer works
Explore the main components of your spectrometer to make sure you understand how it works. Use the questions below to guide you. You could discuss the questions with your group, research them online, ask your teacher or test modifications to your spectrometer to find the answers.
The slit
What is the purpose of the slit?



Why should the slit be as narrow as possible?


The diffraction grating
What is the purpose of the diffraction grating?


Predict what you think will happen if the diffraction grating is misaligned by 90°.




Calibrate your spectrometer
Your spectrometer is useful to allow you to see an emission spectrum of light. However, you currently have no way of measuring which wavelengths of light you are seeing. If you want a more precise instrument that can identify which wavelengths are present, you need to calibrate your spectrometer. 
Calibration is the process of configuring an instrument so that it can accurately measure something. 
Method
Cut out a strip of graph paper and tape it inside your spectrometer, next to the slit, as shown in the diagram. 
Point your spectrometer at a source of white light (for example, an incandescent lamp) and notice where the emission spectrum of this light is located on the graph paper. 
Mark on the graph paper the beginning and the end points of the emission spectrum that you see inside your spectrometer. 
The blue end of the spectrum will be approximately 400 nm and the red end will be approximately 700 nm. Label the end points of your emission spectrum on the graph paper with these wavelengths. 
Create a scale on your graph paper to indicate each 100 nm mark between 400 nm and 700 nm. 
Your spectrometer is now calibrated. 
Predict the sodium line
When you apply enough heat to salt, the electrons in the sodium atoms are temporarily excited and absorb energy. After a while, the electrons fall back into their original location and emit the extra energy as a bright yellow light. This yellow light has a wavelength of approximately 589 nm. 
On an emission spectrum, the location at 589 nm is called the ‘sodium line’. 
You will now predict the location of the sodium line and then check your prediction using your spectrometer to observe heated sodium.
Equipment
A small ceramic bowl
A heat mat
20 mL of ethanol
10 mL of saturated salt solution
Matches
An oven mitt
A white tile 
Note: Your teacher may prepare the heated sodium for you.
Method
Use the scale you created on your graph paper to predict where the sodium line is. Mark this location on your graph paper.
Place the ceramic bowl on the heat mat.
Add 20 mL of ethanol to the bowl.
Add 10 mL of saturated salt solution to the ethanol.
Being careful to ensure your ceramic bowl is well away from fire hazards, use a match to light up the ethanol/saturated salt solution. 
While the solution is burning, use your spectrometer to observe the flame. Look for a bright yellow line in the emission spectrum. This is the sodium line. 
Compare the location of sodium line of the solution with your prediction.
While wearing the oven mitt, extinguish the burning solution by carefully placing the white tile on top of the ceramic bowl to prevent oxygen fuelling the flame. 
Caution: The ceramic bowl and tile will be very hot. Leave your equipment in a safe place to cool before packing up. 
Discussion and reflection
Describe the accuracy of your prediction of the sodium line location. Explain what this tells you about how precisely your instrument is calibrated.




Describe any other colours that you saw in the emission spectrum of the solution. Explain why these other colours could be seen.




Extension activity
Predict what you think would happen to the emission spectrum in your spectrometer if you doubled the length of the box (and therefore doubled the distance between the slit and the diffraction grating). 




Construct a double-length spectrometer to test your prediction.

Terrarium biosphere
The biosphere comprises all living things on Earth including animals, plants, fungi and microorganisms. 
The organisms of the biosphere would not be able survive without the interactions that are made between the biosphere, the lithosphere (the Earth’s mantle and crust), the hydrosphere (all water on Earth) and the atmosphere (layer of gases surrounding Earth). Through these interactions, matter that is critical to life such as carbon, water, nitrogen, and other nutrients can be exchanged, used and cycled by different organisms for survival.
Build a terrarium
Aim
To build your own terrarium to examine how matter (such as carbon) is cycled through the Earth’s spheres. You will also investigate what conditions can affect the cycling of nutrients. 
Materials
A clean, clear glass jar with a lid (e.g. a mason jar, 500 mL to 1 L in size)
Potting mix or soil
Pebbles 
Charcoal mix or fragments
A selection of small plants (e.g. fittonia, ferns, peperomia)
Long tweezers
Moss or algae 
100 mL of water from a nearby pond or outdoor water source 
Distilled water
Scissors
Label
Sticky tape
Method
Place the pebbles/gravel at the base of the jar. This bottom layer should be roughly 2–3 cm in height (this will vary depending on the size of the jar).
Add potting mix or soil to the jar until it is approximately one-third full of soil. 
Sprinkle some charcoal mix or fragments on top of the soil layer. 
Carefully place a selection of plants in the soil so their roots are submerged into the soil. You might like to do this with tweezers. Do not overcrowd the jar with plants. 
Cover the exposed soil surrounding the plants with a layer of moss or algae. 
Add 50 mL (100 mL if you have a larger jar) of the pond water to the jar. Then add distilled water so that the plants are given a good watering but are not completely submerged in water. (You might want to ask your teacher for guidance on this.)
Seal the jar with the lid, label it with your name and place the terrarium near a window in the classroom. Monitor the jar over the next few weeks. 
Monitoring your terrarium
The organisms in your terrarium will take some time to adapt to their new environment. If your plants are wilting, open the jar and spray the plants with water, and then reseal it.
Over the next two to three weeks, monitor your terrarium to observe any changes to the environment (e.g. condensation, size of the plants, growth of any new species). Fill in your observations in the table below. 

Observations

After one week

After three weeks



Analyse the components of your terrarium

The lithosphere

Why there were no observable changes to the lithosphere you created in your terrarium?


The biosphere

Why was it necessary to place the terrarium near a window?


Why was pond water added to your terrarium? Explain how this impacts your biosphere.


The hydrosphere
Throughout the course of your observations, you might have noticed a build-up of water droplets along the sides and top of the terrarium. How does this occur and why is it important for the life that exists in your biosphere?


The atmosphere
What gases form the atmosphere of the environment you have created?


The terrarium was sealed so that no gases could enter or escape, but the plants were still able to photosynthesise and grow. How did the plants survive despite the initial low levels of CO2 in the terrarium?


Make predictions about your terrarium
Some of the plants in your terrarium would have grown from the first week to the final week of observations. Predict what would happen to the growth of your plants if you continued to monitor your terrarium for another three months. Justify your prediction. 





Predict what would happen if you placed your terrarium outside, in full sunlight. Describe how this would affect the temperature inside the terrarium. 





Predict what would happen if you added several animals, such as caterpillars or snails, to your terrarium. Describe the impact this would have on the survival of the plants and the cycling of matter inside the terrarium.

Extending science worksheet
Soundproofing
Cities are noisy places. The constant assault of noise on the ears of city dwellers has been found to have had an impact on hearing abilities. There are estimates that as many as 1 in 6 adults who live in cities have some form of hearing loss. Engineers who specialise in sound are called acoustic engineers. One of their common tasks is to reduce the amount of noise that enters buildings and workplaces. 
When a sound wave travelling through the air hits a solid material, some of the sound energy is reflected back towards the source, some of it is transmitted through the material and some of it is absorbed by the material (and turned into heat energy). 

Different materials reflect, transmit and absorb sound to different extents. Acoustic engineers make use of these properties to minimise the transmission of sound. This is called soundproofing. 
Investigate soundproofing materials 
Aim
To investigate which materials have good soundproofing properties
Materials
Device that can emit sounds at specific frequencies (e.g. tone emitter or mobile phone app)
Decibel meter (e.g. handheld meter or mobile phone app)
Shoebox 
Range of soundproofing materials (e.g. polystyrene, cotton wool, rubber, cardboard, fabric, foil, bubble wrap)
Method
Find a quiet location to carry out your experiment.
Place the sound-emitting device inside the shoebox. Leave the lid off. 
Place the decibel meter about 1 metre away from the sound-emitting device.
Set the sound-emitting device to a frequency of 100 Hz and generate a loud tone. (Note: This volume level must be kept constant for the rest of the experiment.)
Measure the level of the sound generated by the sound-emitting device in decibels (dB) and record it in the table in the Data and results section. 
Adjust the sound-emitting device to 500 Hz, measure the sound in decibels and record it in the table. 
Adjust the sound-emitting device to 1000 Hz, measure the sound in decibels and record it in the table. 
Place the lid on the shoebox and repeat your measurements at the three different frequencies. Record your results in the table. 
Choose five different soundproofing materials and list them in the table. For each material, use it to cover the box and repeat the measurements at the three frequencies. Record your results in the table.

Discussion and reflection
Rank the soundproofing materials in order from least soundproof to most soundproof.




Using the words “reflection”, “absorption” and “transmission”, describe what is happening to the noise coming from the sound-emitting device as it travels through the shoebox and the soundproofing material and arrives at the decibel meter. 





Identify the characteristics of the materials that were best at soundproofing. Describe what they have in common. In particular, consider the density of the materials (how compact they are). 





Identify the characteristics of the materials that were worst at soundproofing. Describe what they have in common. Again, consider the density of the materials.





Analyse the effect of the soundproofing materials at different frequencies. Describe the effect, if any, the frequency of the sounds had on the amount of sound energy that was absorbed by the soundproofing materials. 





Imagine you are an acoustic engineer, and it is your job to soundproof a drum rehearsal room. The only materials you have to use are glass, wood and rubber. Identify which of these soundproofing materials you would use and why. Using what you have learnt about the characteristics of a good soundproofing material, explain why your chosen material is best. 





Extension activity: The Epidaurus Theatre – an acoustic masterpiece
As well as reducing sound, acoustic engineers must sometimes enhance sound, such as in concert halls and theatres. A lot of scientific planning goes into choosing the materials and shapes in modern theatres to optimise how sound waves travel from the stage to the audience in a systematic manner. 
In the 4th century BCE, long before the nature of sound waves was well understood, a theatre was built in Epidaurus in Greece that is generally accepted to be an acoustic masterpiece. In this large, open-air theatre, audiences of up to 14,000 people can easily hear actors and musicians from the back seats … without microphones!

Investigate and describe the secret behind the Epidaurus Theatre’s amazing sound properties.

The rock cycle
Key terms
deposition
the process in which sediment from different forms of weathering accumulates in layers 
frost shattering
a process of weathering in which repeated freezing and melting of water expands cracks in rocks, so that eventually part of the rock splits off 
rock cycle
the process of formation and destruction of different rock types
tor
a large, round rock produced by onion-skin weathering 
What is weathering?


What is erosion?

What is onion-skin weathering?

Next to each image, write whether it is an example of onion-skin weathering, frost shattering or abrasion.






Create a flow chart using the following sentences.
Water expands and pushes against the crack in the rock.
Ice melts and water fills the crack again.
Water freezes in the crack of a rock at night.
The crack becomes larger.


Word detective
Order us!
Put the sentences into the correct order in the cartoon strip, and illustrate each step.
As the temperature keeps rising, the rock becomes magma.
The rock gets hotter and experiences more pressure as it gets deeper. It turns into a metamorphic rock.
Sediments form on top of the rock, causing it to sink deeper.
Magma flows to a volcano, where it becomes lava as it exits the volcano.
A rock is on the Earth’s surface.
When the lava cools, it hardens to become an igneous rock.

Plate tectonics
Key terms
continental drift
the continuous movement of the continents over time 
continental shelf
a flat area under shallow ocean water at the edge of a continent
convection
the transfer of thermal energy by the movement of molecules in air or liquid from one place to another
convection current
the current or flow of air or liquid that results from the transfer of thermal energy through convection 
plate tectonics
the theory that the surface of Earth consists of a series of plates that are continually moving due to convection, ridge push and slab pull
ridge push
the force pushing the edges of tectonic plates away from each other when a ridge crest has formed
slab pull
the force pulling a tectonic plate beneath a less dense tectonic plate
subduction
the movement of one tectonic plate under another tectonic plate

Plate boundaries
Key terms
converging boundary
the boundary between two tectonic plates that are moving together
diverging boundary
the boundary between two tectonic plates that are moving apart 
fault
a fracture in rock where the tectonic plates have moved
mid-ocean ridge
a series of underwater mountains that form as a result of tectonic plates moving apart and allowing magma to rise to the surface 
ocean trench
a deep ditch under the ocean along a tectonic plate boundary 
rift valley
a deep valley that forms as a result of tectonic plates moving apart on land 
transforming boundary
the boundary between two tectonic plates that are sliding past each other 
Summarise tectonic plate boundary movement in the following table. Some of them have been done for you. 

Transforming
Converging
Diverging
Direction of movement (use arrows)

→  ←

Description of movement


Hot rising mantle rock from deep within Earth might be the first step in a continent breaking apart. As the mantle rock rises, the continental crust is lifted and thins out. Cracks form and large slabs of rock sink into the earth.
What types of tectonic plates are involved?
Continental plates and oceanic plates


Effect of the movement (i.e. what does it result in?)

Trenches, volcanoes and mountains

Define a fault.


What does subduction create?


Describe how a rift valley is formed.


Word detective
Matching meaning
Fill in the type of plate, then match each type to its explanation by drawing a line between them. 
Diagram
Types of plates
Explanation


When oceanic crust collides with continental crust, the oceanic landform is pushed downwards into the mantle because it is denser. This is known as subduction.


When two continental plates collide, they have similar densities, so no subduction takes place. Instead, the edges of the two plates crumple and fold into high mountain ranges.


When two oceanic plates collide, the older, denser crust subducts below the newer crust, creating a deep ocean trench. The subduction also creates a line of undersea volcanoes that may reach above the ocean surface.

Extend your understanding 
Consider for a moment the Sun and our planet Earth. They do not touch each other, so thermal energy cannot be transferred from the Sun to Earth by conduction. Neither can heat be transferred to Earth from the Sun by convection as the space between them is essentially a vacuum. However, you can stand with your back to the Sun on a cold day and feel yourself begin to warm up. If it is not by conduction or convection, how does thermal energy from the Sun reach Earth? The answer is via radiation emitted by the Sun.
The Sun emits electromagnetic radiation that is absorbed when it reaches Earth. This absorption of electromagnetic radiation by particles on Earth causes them to move more rapidly, thus heating them.
All objects transfer some heat by emitting radiation. The hotter an object is, the more heat it radiates. Remember that the radiation itself is not hot – it is the absorption of the radiation by an object that causes it to heat up.

Democritus’ model of the atom was a theoretical model. Thompson’s model was an evidence-based model. Compare these two types of models from the descriptions. Use the graphic organiser on the next page to list their similarities and differences.
Democritus was a natural philosopher. Natural philosophers believed that two things made up the natural world: atoms and the void. Atoms were completely solid, with no gaps; they came in a variety of sizes and shapes, were indivisible and infinite in number. Atoms moved about in the void, repelling each other when they collided or combining into clusters. The clusters formed by tiny hooks or barbs on the surface that held the cluster together. All changes in the visible world were a result of these interactions. Atoms could change places, but could not be changed, destroyed or created from nothing.
Berryman, S. (2016) “Democritus”, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, accessed at https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/democritus/
Before Thomson’s model, the accepted model of the atom did not have any charged particles, because the atom was considered to be indivisible. Thomson discovered the electron, a subatomic particle, when experimenting with a cathode-ray tube. To account for electrons, he devised a new model, with negatively charged particles spread throughout the solid positive mass of the atom, like raisins in a plum pudding.
American Board for Certification of Teacher Excellence (ABCTE) (2007) “Modern atomic theory: Models”, accessed at http://www.abcte.org/files/previews/chemistry/s1_p5.html
If you want to know more about Democritus’ idea of the atom or Thomson’s atomic model, do some research online.

Atoms, elements and the periodic table
Research and outline how our understanding of the structure of atoms has changed as a result of Rutherford’s gold foil experiment.








In Niels Bohr’s model of the atom, he proposed that electrons orbit in distinct electron shells. Research and describe the current understanding of the atomic structure.










Döberiner was the first to look at patterns of the different elements. Research and describe the patterns he considered and how he arranged the elements. 




The Russian chemist Mendeleev also looked at the elements. Research this chemist and comment on the significance of his contribution.

Assess the contributions of the chemists in question 3 to the periodic table.








Comment on whether you think these chemists understood the electron orbits as proposed by Neils Bohr when they were organising the periodic table. 









Identify the properties (factors) the chemists considered when organising the elements.

pure substance

Communicating with your audience
When you are sick, you visit the doctor. Doctors have many years of training to ask questions, observe disease symptoms, diagnose disease and decide if medication is needed. phloem
the vascular tissue in plant stems that carries sugars around the plant 
root
a plant organ involved in absorbing nutrients and water
stem
an organ that transports materials around a plant
transpiration
the process of water evaporating from plant leaves; causes water to move up through the plant from the roots 
vascular bundle
a group of tubes in plant stems that carry water and nutrients around the plant 
xylem
the tissue in plants that carries water from the roots to the rest of the plant

Key term 
Definition 

Water and minerals are transported through these vessels in a plant 

The protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and organs in the body, and transfers carbon dioxide back to the lungs 

The outer layer of a root in a plant 

A circulatory system that has vessels in which the blood remains contained

Identify which of the following is the most correct statement about transport systems in plants.
Plants use a closed circulatory system to transport oxygen to leaves and remove carbon dioxide.
Water moves from the soil into the root hairs, then across the root cortex to the vascular tissue. Water and minerals are then drawn up the stem to the leaves via the xylem vessels, while the phloem vessels transport food from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
Water moves from the soil into the root hairs, then across the root cortex to the vascular tissue. Water and minerals are then drawn up the stem to the leaves via the phloem vessels, while the xylem vessels transport food from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
Small plants use an open circulatory system to transport water from the soil to the leaves.
Identify which of the following is the most correct statement about transport systems in an insect. 
All insects use a closed circulatory system to transport oxygen and carbon dioxide around their body.
All insects, regardless of size, use diffusion through spiracles and an open circulatory system for nutrients.
Arthropods use an open circulatory system, while all vertebrates and some invertebrates use a closed circulatory system.
Arthropods use a closed circulatory system, while all vertebrates and some invertebrates use an open circulatory system.

uploads/science/Oxford/Year 8/Oxford/SC.searchText:
Oxford Sciences 8 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Extending science worksheet
Can erosion be helpful?
In nature, rocks can be eroded by wind, rain and the trampling feet of animals rubbing across their surfaces over and over. This slow, abrasive erosion can create all sorts of interesting shapes and patterns. 
Manufacturing engineers use the idea of abrasive erosion (the repeated rubbing of a surface to wear it away) to create shapes that are useful to us. 
In this task, you are going to explore this idea of using abrasive erosion to make something useful!
Can you make a perfect sphere?
Spheres are useful in wheel bearings, mechanical joints, and even as sculptures or decorations. In this project, your job will be to explore what type of rocks suit the manufacture of a sphere using the concept of erosion. 
A ball-bearing manufacturer, Ball Bearings R Us, wants to install a giant rock sculpture of a sphere outside their headquarters. They will be using abrasive erosion by sanding to create their sphere, and they have asked you to tell them what type of rock they should use. 
They want a sphere that is smooth, perfectly round and does not take too long to manufacture. 
You and your group will use everyday materials to simulate different rock traits and investigate which traits are best suited to the requirements. 
Step 1: Collect your ‘rocks’
Collect a range of materials to test out which traits make a good sphere. Some suggestions are: 
a block of balsa wood
polystyrene packing
a bar of soap
actual rocks
a block of hardened clay
an eraser
any other materials you think might create a good sphere.
Step 2: Describe your ‘rocks’
Use your understanding of the properties of the minerals in rocks to describe your materials as though they were rocks.
Do they have a fine grain, medium grain or coarse grain?
Do they have layers?
How would you describe their hardness?
Material
Description (grain, layers, hardness)
Polystyrene
Coarse grain, no layers, quite soft












Step 3: Start eroding
To investigate which material creates the best sphere, use your sandpaper to start eroding each material. Use the following steps of a scientific experiment to guide you through your investigation.
Aim: 
To investigate how each of the materials responds to erosion by finding which material creates the best sphere 
Hypothesis: 
Write a hypothesis about the materials from your list. Which do you think will make the best sphere? Why do you think that?
Materials: 
your collection of materials
sandpaper
safety gloves
newspaper
Method:
Lay out the newspaper to collect any messy sediment that is created by your sanding. 
Divide the materials between members of your group.
Wearing safety gloves, use the sandpaper to try to erode the materials you have collected into the shape of a sphere. 
Data and results
As you sand each material, make observations about how your materials are responding to the erosion. Your observations could include the answers to questions such as:
Is it breaking apart? 
Is the surface becoming smooth or rough? 
Is the erosion fast or slow? 
Does the sanding require a lot of effort? 
Are you able to attain a sphere shape?
Material

Describe the key observations that you made about how each material was affected by the sandpaper erosion.
Describe the rock traits of each material that caused it to behave the way it did.
Identify the material that was most suitable for making a sphere. Explain why you made this conclusion. Compare your hypothesis to the conclusion.
Describe the traits that you would look for in terms of grain, layering and hardness, if you were to make a sphere out of an actual rock.











Conclusion

Extending science worksheet
Shake, rattle and record
When the pressure that has built up between tectonic plates is suddenly released, it can cause an earthquake. Scientists use a special machine called a seismograph to measure the magnitude of movement in the Earth (the seismic waves) that an earthquake causes. 
Some of the earliest seismographs were created more than 2000 years ago in China using small bronze balls that would simply drop on to a surface to make a noise when the Earth shook. Today, seismographs are finely tuned machines that can tell scientists about the magnitude of seismic waves in great detail. 
In this task, you will create your own simple seismograph and explore how it works. This activity is best carried out in a group. 

Build your seismograph 
You will need the following materials to build your seismograph:
Free-standing table
Retort stand and clamp
Two retort stand clamps
Metal spring
Horseshoe magnet
Plastic cup
String
Marbles or stones
Pencil (or pen)
Long thin strips of butcher’s paper
The following steps will guide you through the construction of your seismograph.
Firmly clamp the base of your retort stand to your table.
Using one of the retort stand clamps, attach the spring to the top of the retort stand. 
Using the other retort stand clamp, attach the horseshoe magnet so that it straddles the spring.
Make a small hole in the bottom of your cup and push the pencil through it, then fill up the cup with marbles or other heavy material to secure your pencil in place. 
Attach a string handle to your cup either with strong tape or by punching a small hole in opposite sides of the cup and tying the string through these holes. 
Hang the cup onto the bottom of the spring. 
Adjust the heights of your clamps so that the tip of your pencil is just touching the base of the retort stand. If required, tape your pencil in place at the bottom of the cup to keep it secure. 
Test your seismograph 
Now test your seismograph. First, place one end of a strip of butcher’s paper under the pencil and slowly drag it across the retort stand so that a line appears on the paper. Once you have a good straight line appearing, try this again with a fresh piece of paper, but this time, get one member of your group to gently wobble the table as you pull to create a ‘table earthquake’. 
Experiment with different magnitudes of ‘table earthquakes’ to see how your seismograph responds. 
Investigate and improve your seismograph
There are lots of different parts required for this seismograph and it is quite likely that some of these things are not working perfectly. You will now analyse your seismograph, identify the problems and consider ways to improve the design. 
Analyse the seismograph
Before you can improve on the design, you must be sure you understand everything about it. Discuss the questions below with your group to make sure you understand each component in the seismograph. 
You might like to try some tests with your seismograph. Use the internet, your teacher or other resources to confirm your understanding. Write notes to record your thinking.
The spring
Describe the purpose of the spring. 


Suggest why it must be a metal spring.


Describe what might happen if a metal wire be used instead. (You might like to try this out to find out.)





The horseshoe magnet
Describe the purpose of the horseshoe magnet. 


Describe what would happen if you removed the magnet. (You might like to try this to find out.)



The cup
Describe the purpose of the marbles in the cup. 


Describe what would happen if you removed the marbles. (You might like to try this to find out.)



Identify problems
Now you understand how each component of the seismograph works, think about the problems you have encountered in its use. Is the paper wide enough? Is the paper hard to guide? Does the cup swing too much? Does the spring bounce too much? Is the pencil too loose in the cup?
Note down any problems you found with your seismograph that impacts on how well it measures ‘table earthquakes’.






Improve the design
For each of the problems you have identified, brainstorm possible ways to improve the seismograph with your group. Write down all your ideas, no matter how silly or unlikely. 









Now choose your best improvement idea for each problem and circle it. Implement these ideas into the seismograph design and then test your improved design with different magnitude table earthquakes.
Discussion and reflection
Compare how the machine worked before and after your improvements.






Identify which improvement made the most difference. Identify which improvement made the least difference. 









Describe the next improvement that you would like to try next (if you had time).







Your seismograph does not have a scale. Describe how you would describe the magnitude of your table earthquakes without a scale. 








Describe the Richter scale.








To detect the origin of an earthquake (i.e. the location where it occurred), you need the data from three seismographs in different locations. Discuss why this would be needed with your group and record your ideas below.

Grape catapult
Before humans used gunpowder and explosives to fire things through the air, they used catapults. The original concept of a catapult is attributed to the Greeks, who are said to have invented the idea as a modification of the crossbow. Like many technologies, the design and use of catapults flourished during times of war. They were still being used in combat during World War I, to fire grenades into enemy trenches. 
Catapults are an energy transformation machine. In essence, they transform the elastic potential energy in a springy material into kinetic energy in a flying object. 
In this task, you will design a way to harness the elastic potential energy of a rubber band to create a grape catapult that will be as accurate as possible.
The first step will be to create a grape target. On a large piece of butcher’s paper, create a target similar to the one shown and stick this up on a wall. 
You will also need the following materials to design and make your grape catapult:
Up to 15 ice-cream sticks 
1 or 2 rubber bands
1 plastic spoon
Hot-glue gun
To guide you in your design, you will use the steps of the engineering design process. The engineering design process has five major steps:
Discover. Consider the problem or objective from all angles, research it and brainstorm ideas. 
Ideate. Develop a possible solution and design a prototype.
Build. Build the prototype.
Test. Evaluate the prototype to see if it meets the objective.
Improve. From the test results, identify how to make your design better.
Discover
Your objective is to create a grape catapult from the materials provided that is as accurate as possible.
First, think about this objective and how you will tackle it. Follow the questions in the table below to help guide your thinking. Add any additional questions of your own at the end.
Question
Notes
Draw a picture of what comes to mind when you think of a catapult.
What are some of the features that you have drawn?

Many ice-cream-stick catapult designs already exist. Research some existing designs and note down the features that you see. What do they have in common?

Most catapults include a lever of some type. What types of levers are possible? In particular, think about where the fulcrum (or pivot point) could be located along the lever.


Most catapults include a base of some type to support the lever. What designs are possible for the base of a catapult? Explore the options.

Other questions:

Ideate
Now that you have done some thinking, brainstorm ideas for a catapult design using only the materials you have been assigned. Think specifically about the base, the lever and how your catapult will transform the elastic potential energy into kinetic energy. 








Choose your best idea and develop it further. Write up a description of your catapult design including a labelled diagram of how it works. Use the following questions to help you.
What shape will your base be?
If you are using a lever, how will it be secured and where will the fulcrum be located?
What will be used to house the projectile grape before take-off?
How will you be able to vary your catapult launch characteristics (direction and force) to optimise the accuracy of the grape’s flight path?
What safety issues are involved in creating and testing your catapult?








Draw a diagram of your design here.





Build
Build a prototype of your catapult, being especially careful with the hot-glue gun. A prototype is a “first try” to test if your concept will work. Write down the steps you took to build your prototype below. 








Test
Once your catapult is created, check to see if it works by placing it 1 metre from your target on the wall. Fire a few grapes at the wall and write down your observations about where they hit the target, if at all. If there are problems, note these down. 




Improve
Based on your test observations, how could you improve your design? Note down any ideas you have that could make it better. 




Repeat steps 4 and 5 to implement as many of your improvement ideas as possible in the time you have.
Data and results
Gather data on the accuracy of your catapult by firing six grapes at the target (from 1 metre in front) and measuring the distance between the centre of the target and the point where each grape hits the target. After each trial, adjust the angle of the catapult and the power of the launch to optimise the results.

Discussion and reflection
Your sixth trial should be the most accurate. Compare your trials to determine if this was correct. 


Compare your results with other groups in the class. Identify the design that was most accurate. Describe the features of the design that made it most accurate.




Draw an energy flow diagram to show the path of the energy in your catapult system. Start with the energy that is transferred from your hand when you stretch the rubber band and finish with the energy that is transferred when the grape hits the target.

Build a material for a mission
As a scientist, your job goes far beyond just learning facts – your knowledge helps solve real-world problems. Imagine you’ve been hired by a team of engineers to design a new underwater exploration robot. In this activity, you’ll apply everything you’ve learned about atoms, elements and the periodic table to design the perfect material for a robot capable of exploring the deepest parts of the ocean!

Engineering chemical reactions
Milk is made up of a mixture of particles including fats, water and different small proteins including casein. These particles can be separated in different ways to make cream, butter, ice cream and polymer plastic. The first three you might have known, but making polymer plastic from milk is rare today. Before World War II, buttons and simple jewellery were made from the casein in milk. 
When you heat milk, it allows the casein to change its shape. Adding vinegar (an acid) makes the casein arrange itself into a shape – a bit like building blocks. These blocks can then join together to make long strands called polymers. These long strands can slide past each other easily like strands of spaghetti. 
In this task, you will explore the chemical production of polymer plastic from milk. You will start with the following pre-experiment to test the process involved. This task is best done as a group. 
Pre-experiment: Manufacturing plastic from milk
Aim:
To create a polymer plastic from milk
Materials:
50 mL full cream milk 
Clean washcloth 
Vinegar 
Beaker 
Funnel 
Measuring cylinder 
Scales 
Teaspoon 
60°C water bath 
Method:
Add the milk to a beaker. 
Place the beaker of milk in the water bath for 10 minutes. 
Add 2 teaspoons of vinegar into the warm milk and stir gently with the spoon. 
Observe the mixture as it starts to curdle. The liquid part is called whey. The solids are called curds – these are the molecules of casein forming a polymer. 
Place the clean cloth inside the funnel. 
Gently tip the curds and whey into the cloth, catching the casein curds in the cloth. 
Weigh your casein plastic on the scales and enter your data into the table in the Data and results section. 
Knead the casein plastic with your fingers. Describe the consistency of the material in the table in the Data and results section.
Improving the manufacturing process
Chemical engineers are interested in the way that materials can be changed into useful products. They research the properties of raw materials, and design and evaluate the processes used to produce the products. Their role often involves improving the manufacturing process so that the amount of product is maximised, improving the quality of the product and ensuring that the manufacturing process is safe and cost-effective.
Imagine your group has been employed by the casein plastic button company to improve their product at minimum cost. There are two ways you can improve your product: 
Maximise the amount of product (by weight) that can be produced from 50 mL of milk. 
Improve the consistency of the product so that no cracks appear in the final dried buttons. 
Use the following steps to guide you through the improvement process. 
Step 1: Review the cost of materials
The material available for you to use for manufacturing casein have the following costs:

Step 2: Modify a variable
Consider the following questions: What variables could you change in your manufacturing process to either maximise the amount of product or improve the consistency? In what way could you modify these variables and how would this affect the cost?
You must now choose, as a group, how you will change variables to explore improvements in the manufacturing process. 
In your group, decide which variable from the pre-experiment to modify first and write a description of this first modification scenario in the table in the Data and results section. Calculate the cost of this first modification scenario and add it to the table. 
Step 3: Investigate 
Repeat the pre-experiment with the modification scenario you have decided on. Enter your results in the table. 
Step 4: Clean and repeat
Having observed the results of your first modification scenario, decide what you will modify next and repeat steps 2 and 3. You will need to clean your equipment before repeating the experiment. Continue modifying your variables, one at a time, until you feel your manufacturing process has been considerably improved at a reasonable cost. Record your results for each modification in the table.

Describe any improvements you achieved in the manufacturing process.




Describe the effect your improvements had on the cost of the process.




Evaluate if the cost impact of your improvement was worth it. Calculate the effect your improvement would have on the price of the plastic buttons.




Describe what you could measure to determine if the improvement has been worthwhile.

Extension activity

How clean are your hands?
Bacteria are organisms that are made up of only one cell. They reproduce very quickly by splitting into two – a process called binary fission. This reproduction process can take just minutes to occur, meaning one bacterial cell can turn into millions of cells in a few hours. 
Some bacteria are harmless, or even helpful, to humans. However, there are also bacteria that are harmful and dangerous. Bacteria is responsible for infections such as pneumonia, meningitis and food poisoning.
It is important that harmful bacteria on our bodies are minimised to reduce the risk of them getting inside us and making us sick. The primary method of reducing harmful bacteria on the skin is simply by cleaning ourselves. Keeping our skin clean is vitally important in places such as hospitals where there are people who are in a weakened condition or have wounds that make them susceptible to a bacterial infection. 
In this activity, you will be asked to advise the manager of a hospital of the method of hand cleaning that should be enforced to minimise the risk of bacteria breeding. You will compare three methods of hand cleaning to find out which is most effective. 
This activity is best done as a group.
Experiment: Investigation of hand-cleaning methods 
Aim:
To find the most effective hand-cleaning method
Materials:
4 prepared agar plates and lids
4 cotton swabs
Water
Soap
Antibacterial gel
Camera
Method: 
Choose one member of your group to be your subject. They will provide bacteria samples from their hands. 
Using the first cotton swab, rub the palm of the subject’s right hand with the swab and then gently rub the swab on the first agar plate. Replace the agar plate lid securely and label it: “control – no cleaning”.
Next, help your subject clean their right hand with soap and water. Using another cotton swab, rub the palm of the subject’s right hand again and then gently rub this swab on the second agar plate. Replace the agar plate lid securely and label it: “soap and water”.
Next, help your subject clean their left hand with antibacterial gel. Using a third cotton swab, rub the palm of the subject’s left hand and gently rub this swab on the third agar plate. Replace the agar plate lid securely and label it: “antibacterial gel”.
Now, help your subject clean their right hand again, this time with antibacterial gel.
Using the last cotton swab, rub the palm of the subject’s right hand again and gently rub this swab on the last agar plate. Replace the agar plate lid securely and label it: “soap and water plus antibacterial gel”.
Check your plates every two days and record photos of any bacterial growth you observe.

Imagine that soap costs 25 cents per wash and antibacterial gel costs 35 cents per wash. The hospital is on a tight budget and any money saved can go towards saving patients. They want to minimise cost, but not jeopardise cleanliness. Describe the action that you would recommend.




Now imagine these costs reversed: soap costs 35 cents per wash and antibacterial gel costs 25 cents per wash. Describe if/how your advice would change. 





Extension activity: Antibiotics and super-bugs
Once harmful bacteria have made their way inside our bodies, one of the most common ways to reduce the harmful effects is to use antibiotic medication. However, the high use of antibiotics to treat infections, along with the speedy reproduction rate of bacteria, has meant that some bacteria have evolved into “super-bugs” that are almost impossible to kill with regular antibiotics. 
Investigate the emergence of “super-bugs” by examining how they have evolved and make a statement about what they could mean for human health in the future.

Extending science worksheet
Bone density
Density is the amount of matter in a given space. It is a measure of how tightly packed a material is.
Bone density is the mass of bone per cubic centimetre (the mass per unit volume). It is a measure that tells us about how strong a bone is – the more mass in each cubic centimetre, the less likely it is for the bone to break.
Bone density in humans tends to peak when they are young adults and then starts to decline. However, bone density is positively affected by weight-bearing activities. These are activities where a person uses their muscles to push against the force of gravity. Walking, tennis and weightlifting are all weight-bearing activities. Engaging in weight-bearing forms of exercise will slow down the loss of bone density as a person ages. It will also reduce the chances of developing a medical condition called osteoporosis, which occurs when bones lose too much density. Osteoporosis is typically associated with age as well as hormonal changes, or a deficiency of calcium or vitamin D.
In this task, you will investigate how much force is required to break the bones of different animals with different bone densities. 
Bone density experiment
Aim:
To measure the relationship between bone density and the force required to break a bone
Materials:
Chicken rib bone
Lamb or pig rib bone
Fish rib bone
Kitchen scales
Beaker
Water
Hanging weights secured with fishing line
Retort stands or clamps
Method:
Measure the mass in kilograms of each bone with the kitchen scales and record it in the table in the Data and results section. Be sure to record it in kilograms, not grams. 
Fill up the beaker to a chosen volume that will provide enough water to submerge the bones. 
Submerge each bone, one by one, into the water. Note by how much the volume measurement of the water in the beaker increases when the bone is fully submerged. This is the volume of the bone in millilitres (mL). 
In the table, record the volume of each bone in cm3 (note that 1 mL = 1 cm3).
Use the results to calculate the density of each bone and write it in the table. The density is the mass (kg) divided by the volume (cm3). 
Use the clamps to secure the bones horizontally to the table.
Attach hanging weights to the centre of the secured bone with fishing line. Slowly increase the amount of weight hanging from the bone until the bone breaks. 
In the Data and results section, record the mass of the weights (in kilograms) required to break each bone.
Use these results to calculate the force that was required to break the bones. Force is the mass multiplied by the acceleration due to gravity (which is approximately 9.8 m/s2).
Underneath your results tables, graph the bone density against the force required to break the bone.

Nature vs nurture
While the genes you inherit from your mother and father determine a lot of your own traits, they don’t determine everything. Factors in your environment, such as lifestyle and upbringing, will also play a big part in how you grow and develop. The genetic factors that contribute to the characteristics of an organism are called “nature factors” and the environmental factors are called “nurture factors”. Scientists have debated the relative importance of nature and nurture factors for decades. 
Plants can also be the product of both nature and nurture. Their development will depend on the genetic makeup of their parent plants (nature) as well as the characteristics of their environment (nurture).
The nurture of sunflowers
While most sunflower seeds are not genetically identical, seeds of the same breed are very similar and produce very similar-looking seedlings. In this task, you will use genetically similar sunflower seeds to explore the impact of nurture factors on the growth and development of seedlings. 
Experiment: The effect of nurture
Aim:
To investigate the effect of environmental conditions on the development of sunflower plants
Materials:
8 sunflower seeds
8 seedling pots or yoghurt tubs
Soil
Liquid fertiliser 
Water
Ruler

Method: 
Fill the eight seedling pots or yoghurt tubs with soil.
Insert one sunflower seed in each pot, approximately 1 cm below the surface of the soil.
Separate your pots into two groups of four. Place one group in a sunny location and the other in a dark corner. Label each pot “sun” or “no sun”. 
Within each of these groups, separate the pots into two further subgroups of two. Add liquid fertiliser (in the manner described on the fertiliser packaging) to one of these subgroups. Label the pots with “fertiliser” or “no fertiliser” as appropriate. 
Finally, for the two pots in each subgroup, water one of them well, but don’t add any water to the other. Label the pots with “water” or “no water” as appropriate. 
Leave your plants to grow for three weeks, but add extra water to the pots labelled “water” every two to three days.
Once a week for three weeks, measure the height of your seedlings and record this in the table in the Data and results section.

Discussion and reflection
Describe the effect that sunlight has on the growth of the sunflowers.




Describe the effect that fertiliser has on the growth of the sunflowers.




Describe the effect that water has on the growth of the sunflowers.




Identify other nurture factors that could affect how sunflowers grow and develop.




For this experiment, we assumed that the sunflower seeds were genetically similar. This means we also assumed that we could disregard nature factors. Describe the effect that this assumption could have had on the results if this assumption of genetic similarity was incorrect.




Identify the nurture factors that could affect how you grow and develop.




Do you think nature or nurture factors contribute more to the characteristics shown by plants and animals? Justify your answer by defining nature and nurture, and using an example to describe how they affect the characteristics of the plant or animal. Explain why one factor has a larger impact than the other factor.












Describe why identifying which characteristics are a result of nature or nurture is important to know.
